# Cascades {#sec-cascades}

::: {.callout-note}
This chapter is planned: it states the question and the method. Results will replace the plan as the
analysis is done.
:::

At the top of the ladder are properties of the whole canvas. The first is whether overwrites come in avalanches.

## The question

Add sand to a pile one grain at a time and mostly nothing happens, but sometimes a slide sweeps the pile. Earthquakes,
neuronal activity and forest fires show events of all sizes with no typical scale. Do chains of overwrites on the
canvas (one overwrite provoking nearby ones, which provoke more) have that kind of size distribution?

## Why it matters

If they do, the exponents place r/place next to other systems and can be compared directly. If they do not, that is
equally informative. Either answer is a number other fields can reuse.

## The main risk, built in from the start

Heavy-tailed plots are easy to fake. Thresholded random processes can produce straight lines on log–log axes without
anything critical going on (*established*; Touboul and Destexhe 2010, see @sec-reading). So:

- fit distributions by maximum likelihood and compare against alternatives (log-normal, exponential, stretched
  exponential), following Clauset, Shalizi and Newman (2009);
- run the same cascade definition on time-shuffled and space-shuffled logs, which must not show the same tails;
- report how the result depends on the space and time windows that link overwrites into a cascade.
